newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flynn to renew drive for EU ban on tobacco ads.
newsitem.headline: Flynn to renew drive for EU ban on tobacco ads.

text.p: The European Commission said on Tuesday it would renew attempts to introduce a European Union wide ban on all tobacco advertising, following the new British government's announcement of a national tobacco ad ban.

Last November, EU health ministers shelved efforts to prohibit all tobacco advertising in the face of resistance from a blocking minority of member states, adopting in its place a resolution that simply urged governments to continue and coordinate their anti-smoking efforts.
Britain's former Conservative government sided for many years with the Netherlands, Germany, Greece and Denmark in blocking adoption of a draft EU-wide ban -- COM(92)196.
But if the new British Health Secretary Frank Dobson follows through the national ban with a change of heart in Europe, it would be possible to outlaw tobacco advertising throughout the Union.

At the moment, two thirds of EU countries have some kind of restrictions on publicity for cigarette companies but the Commission has argued that the effectiveness of these bans is limited in the increasingly integrated European market.

A spokeswoman for European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said the Commission was delighted with the change of policy in London and would revive the question of a European ban when EU health ministers meet in Luxembourg on June 5.
But she said she did not expect a more concrete decision on the draft directive until the latter half of the year, when Luxembourg takes over the presidency of the Council of Ministers.

Britain's new Labour government confirmed last week that it planned to outlaw tobacco advertising and followed this up with an announcement on Monday that it was also banning sponsorship of sports events by cigarette companies.

Anti-smoking campaigners welcomed the move but tobacco companies said they were disappointed by a decision they said would not bring a drop in smoking but would deal a blow to many of the nation's favourite fixtures.
Cigarette companies spend millions sponsoring sports such as cricket, golf, darts, rugby, show-jumping and Formula One motor racing.
